description: The plant subject used as the biological system for studying innate immune signaling. In this context, Arabidopsis mutants are analyzed to determine how receptor-mediated pathways contribute to effector-triggered immunity and bacterial resistance.

Arabidopsis PRR mutant background lacking multiple pattern-recognition receptors. This experimental plant population is used to test the requirement of PRR signaling for ETI responses during bacterial challenge.

Arabidopsis co-receptor triple mutant population deficient in key PRR-associated signaling components. These mutants are used to assess impairment of ETI responses and the contribution of PRR co-receptors to immune signaling.

The bacterial challenge used to trigger immune responses in Arabidopsis. Although not a radiation exposure, it functions as the experimental exposure scenario that elicits ETI and associated defense signaling.

A plant innate immune signaling pathway activated by microbial patterns through cell surface PRRs. PTI represents one of the two major immune tiers discussed and is mechanistically linked to downstream defense outputs and ETI potentiation.

A plant immune signaling pathway activated by pathogen effector proteins through intracellular NLR receptors. ETI is the central biological process studied, with impaired responses observed in PRR mutant plants and dependence on early signaling components.
Conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns recognized by cell surface PRRs to initiate PTI. They serve as the upstream molecular cues that activate innate immune signaling in plants.
Cell surface-localized receptors that detect microbial patterns and initiate PTI. PRRs are required for proper ETI responses in this study and are central to the revised model linking PTI and ETI.
Pathogen-derived proteins recognized by intracellular NLR receptors to activate ETI. They represent the molecular trigger for effector-triggered immune signaling.

Intracellular immune receptors that detect pathogen effector proteins and activate ETI. NLRs are part of the core immune architecture discussed and are linked to PTI potentiation and downstream defense outputs.
Early signaling molecules produced during immune activation. In this study, reactive oxygen species production is identified as a critical early event connecting PRR- and NLR-mediated immunity.
A plant NADPH oxidase responsible for reactive oxygen species generation during immune signaling. RBOHD is described as a critical early signaling component linking PRR and NLR pathways.

A receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase required for full activation of RBOHD, gene expression, and bacterial resistance during ETI. BIK1 functions as an important signaling node downstream of PRR-associated immune activation.
Transcriptional response induced during immune signaling. In this study, full activation of gene expression depends on BIK1 during ETI and contributes to defense responses.
The defensive outcome reflecting the plant's ability to resist bacterial infection. It is used as a functional endpoint of ETI signaling and is reduced when key signaling components are impaired.

Key molecular elements of the pattern-triggered immunity pathway whose transcript and/or protein levels are rapidly increased by NLR signaling. They represent the mechanistic bridge by which ETI potentiates PTI.
The overall innate immune framework in plants that supports survival and productivity. It encompasses PTI and ETI and provides the biological context for receptor-mediated defense signaling.

Initial intracellular signaling pathways activated after immune receptor engagement. The text notes that PTI and ETI use distinct early cascades, with RBOHD and BIK1 contributing to these early events.
The biological context in which the immune signaling interactions occur. It provides the infection setting for PTI/ETI interplay and downstream defense outputs.
The plant species used as the biological subject in this study; it is the organism in which circadian clock genes were manipulated to assess effects on iron homeostasis and photosynthetic efficiency.
CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1, a central circadian clock protein/gene in Arabidopsis that regulates iron homeostasis, binds regulatory regions of iron-related genes, and activates their expression.

LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL, a central circadian clock protein/gene in Arabidopsis that functions with CCA1 in maintaining cyclic iron homeostasis and whose loss contributes to reduced iron uptake and altered photosynthetic efficiency.
The endogenous time-keeping machinery that synchronizes metabolism, behavior, and physiology to daily light-dark cycles; it is the broader biological process in which CCA1 and LHY function.
The regulated maintenance of iron balance in plants, including uptake, reduction, transport, and cyclic regulation; this is the central process controlled by CCA1 and LHY in the study.
Iron, an essential micronutrient for plant growth and development; it is the elemental substrate whose uptake and homeostasis are regulated in the study.
The biological process of iron acquisition by the plant, reported to be reduced in the cca1 lhy loss-of-function context.
A physiological performance endpoint measured in the plant; it was reduced when CCA1 and LHY were lost and improved with CCA1 overexpression.
The root-based reduction of ferric iron to a more bioavailable form, described as exhibiting circadian oscillations and being disrupted in the cca1 lhy double mutant.
FERRIC REDUCTION OXIDASE 2, an iron homeostasis gene whose expression shows circadian oscillation and is regulated by CCA1.
IRON-REGULATED TRANSPORTER 1, an iron homeostasis gene involved in iron uptake whose expression oscillates circadianly and is regulated by CCA1.
Rhythmic temporal variation in gene expression and root iron reduction activity driven by the circadian clock; these oscillations are disrupted in the cca1 lhy double mutant.
A mutant Arabidopsis genotype lacking both CCA1 and LHY function, used to demonstrate the loss of circadian regulation of iron homeostasis and associated physiological effects.
Experimental overexpression of CCA1 used as a genetic intervention that produces the opposite phenotype to loss of CCA1/LHY, improving iron-related and photosynthetic outcomes.
A set of iron homeostasis-related genes whose regulatory regions are directly bound by CCA1 and whose expression is activated by CCA1.
The biological subject population discussed in the study, representing the plant systems in which circadian-clock regulation and abiotic stress responses are examined.

Non-living environmental stress conditions affecting plants, including adverse temperature, water imbalance, nutrient deficiency, and salinity; these are the external stress scenarios studied in relation to clock-mediated responses.
A temperature-related abiotic stress condition that perturbs plant growth and development and contributes to the broader abiotic stress context.
A water-stress exposure scenario encompassing drought-like insufficiency or flooding-like excess, both of which are abiotic stressors relevant to plant responses.
A nutrient-limitation stress condition that acts as an abiotic exposure affecting plant physiology and development.
Salt stress exposure condition used in the study as a key abiotic stress affecting seed germination and stress-response regulation.
The endogenous timing system in plants that regulates developmental and metabolic processes and interacts reciprocally with abiotic stress-response pathways.
Broad classes of plant biological processes regulated by the circadian clock and influenced by environmental stress signaling.
A core circadian-clock gene/protein in plants that regulates abiotic stress responses, controls ABF3 expression, and is itself targeted by ABF3 through promoter binding.
A core circadian-clock gene/protein in plants that participates with CCA1 in regulating abiotic stress responses and controlling ABF3 expression.
A key transcription factor in the ABA-signaling pathway that mediates stress-responsive regulation, controls core clock genes, and binds the promoters of CCA1 and LHY.
A plant hormone signaling pathway in which ABF3 functions as a key transcriptional regulator and through which abiotic stress responses are coordinated.
A plant developmental process whose regulation under salinity is influenced by CCA1 and LHY in the study.
Central circadian-clock genes whose expression is controlled by ABF3 in a stress-responsive manner.
The temporal length of the circadian cycle, which is orchestrated by ABF3 under stress-responsive conditions.
The core circadian-clock regulatory system to which ABF3 delivers stress signals by binding the promoters of CCA1 and LHY.
The promoter region targeted by ABF3 for binding, enabling transcriptional regulation of the core clock genes CCA1 and LHY.
The broader environmental context motivating the study, representing the global setting in which abiotic stress pressures on plants are increasing.

The plant organism studied as the biological subject in which circadian clock regulation and chromatin modifications were examined. It provides the genetic and physiological context for the transcriptional rhythms of clock genes.
Endogenous timekeeping mechanisms that coordinate 24 h rhythmic physiology and gene expression. In this study, they regulate transcriptional timing and chromatin state associated with clock genes.
The environmental temporal context of daily light-dark periodicity in which circadian rhythms operate. It frames the rhythmic changes that circadian clocks help organisms anticipate.
A core Arabidopsis clock gene and transcriptional regulator involved in the central oscillator. Its transcriptional rhythm and chromatin modifications were analyzed in relation to circadian control.
A core Arabidopsis clock gene that functions with CCA1 in the central oscillator. Its rhythmic transcription and associated histone modifications were investigated as part of circadian regulation.
A core Arabidopsis clock gene that reciprocally represses and is repressed by CCA1/LHY. It is a key component of the central oscillator and a target of circadian chromatin regulation.
Rhythmic changes in gene transcription over time. In this paper, they describe the oscillatory expression of CCA1, LHY, and TOC1 under circadian control.

Post-translational modifications on histone H3 tails that alter chromatin state and gene accessibility. These modifications were assessed at clock gene loci and linked to circadian transcriptional regulation.

A specific activating histone H3 trimethylation mark associated with transcriptionally active chromatin. It was found enriched at the translational start sites of CCA1, LHY, and TOC1 during peak transcription.

A specific histone H3 acetylation mark associated with open chromatin and active transcription. It was enriched at the translational start sites of the clock genes at times of increased transcription.
A localized genomic feature at the start of translation where histone marks were specifically associated. It serves as the chromatin locus examined for circadian enrichment of H3 modifications.
Specific times within the circadian cycle when gene expression and chromatin marks were measured. They define the temporal context for enrichment of histone modifications.
Distinct light-dark cycle regimes used to test how environmental timing cues affect chromatin changes and transcriptional rhythms. They provide a contextual variable for circadian regulation.

Conditions in which organisms are observed without external time cues, allowing endogenous circadian rhythms to be assessed. They were used to show that histone mark enrichment persists under intrinsic clock control.
Genetically altered Arabidopsis lines overexpressing CCA1 with compromised clock function. They were used to test whether photoperiod-dependent chromatin changes require an intact circadian clock.
Environmental light-dark cycles that provide external timing information. They were shown to signal the establishment of chromatin changes in a clock-gated manner.
Alterations in chromatin state associated with histone modifications at clock gene loci. These changes are regulated by photoperiods and gated by the circadian clock.

The plant species used as the biological subject in this study. It serves as the experimental population in which circadian clock proteins and flowering-time regulation are examined under different light conditions.
A photoperiod exposure scenario characterized by limited daily light duration. In this context it is one of the environmental conditions under which LHY and CCA1 repress floral transition.
A photoperiod exposure scenario with extended daily light duration. It is a key environmental condition for photoperiodic flowering responses and for the regulatory effects of LHY and CCA1.

A constant-light exposure scenario in which plants are grown without a dark period. This condition reveals the accelerated flowering phenotype mediated by LHY and CCA1 and the accumulation of SVP protein in lhy;cca1 plants.
The developmental process by which flowering is regulated according to day length. It is controlled by the GI-CO-FT pathway and modulated by circadian clock proteins in Arabidopsis.
The developmental switch from vegetative growth to flowering. It is repressed by LHY and CCA1 under short-day and long-day conditions and is influenced by SVP-mediated repression of FT expression.
The reproductive developmental endpoint measured in the study. It is accelerated under continuous light by LHY and CCA1 and repressed by SVP and FLOWERING LOCUS C.
The timing of the flowering endpoint, used to describe late-flowering or accelerated-flowering phenotypes. It is regulated by SVP and FLOWERING LOCUS C and altered in lhy;cca1 mutants.
A floral regulator protein that participates in the canonical photoperiodic flowering pathway. It functions upstream in the GI-CO-FT pathway and is part of the conserved flowering regulatory network.
A floral regulator protein involved in photoperiodic flowering control. It acts in the GI-CO-FT pathway and contributes to FT regulation under day-length-dependent conditions.
A key flowering-promoting gene/protein in the photoperiodic pathway. Its expression is promoted by LHY and CCA1 under continuous light and repressed by SVP and FLOWERING LOCUS C.

A circadian clock protein that regulates flowering-time control. It represses floral transition under short-day and long-day conditions, promotes flowering under continuous light, and reduces SVP abundance to support FT expression.

A circadian clock protein that functions with LHY in flowering regulation. It represses floral transition under short-day and long-day conditions, promotes flowering under continuous light, and contributes to reduced SVP accumulation.
The canonical photoperiodic flowering pathway composed of GI, CO, and FT. It is highly conserved in plants and mediates day-length-dependent flowering responses.

A MADS box transcription factor that acts as a flowering repressor. Its mutations suppress the late-flowering phenotype of lhy;cca1 under continuous light, and its protein accumulates in lhy;cca1 plants.
The protein family classification for SVP, indicating its role as a transcriptional regulator in flowering control. This molecular feature is relevant to repression of flowering time.
A flowering regulator protein that interacts with SVP. It acts as a partially redundant repressor of flowering time together with SVP.

A genetic mutant plant population lacking both LHY and CCA1 function. It exhibits a late-flowering phenotype under continuous light and is used to infer the roles of these circadian proteins in flowering regulation.
A genetic analysis approach used to identify suppressor mutations affecting the late-flowering phenotype of the lhy;cca1 double mutant. It provides evidence linking SVP to flowering-time control.
A protein-protein interaction assay used to test physical interaction between SVP and FLOWERING LOCUS C. It supports the mechanistic relationship between these flowering regulators.
A study method used to infer functional relationships among flowering regulators. In this paper it indicates that SVP and FLOWERING LOCUS C act as partially redundant repressors of flowering time.

Model plant subject used in the study to examine how twilight length influences growth, flowering time, and downstream molecular responses. It is the biological system in which the clock-gene and photoreceptor pathways were analyzed.

Experimental growth environment used to manipulate light conditions and assess plant responses under controlled twilight and photoperiod regimes. It provides the context for the observed growth and flowering phenotypes.

The duration of twilight, treated here as an environmental light-exposure scenario that varies across conditions and is experimentally manipulated to study its effects on plant development and molecular pathways.

The length of the light/dark cycle used as a comparative environmental light scenario. In the study, twilight length was compared against equivalent changes in photoperiod to assess relative sensitivity.
An environmental variable mentioned as one of the major seasonal and latitudinal factors affecting plant responses, though not the primary manipulated factor in this study.
A series of progressively truncated light-cycle conditions lacking twilight, used to isolate the effect of twilight duration from overall photoperiod changes.
A developmental endpoint reflecting plant biomass or vegetative development, reported as being affected by twilight length in Arabidopsis.
A key developmental endpoint indicating the timing of reproductive transition in Arabidopsis, shown to be modulated by twilight length through clock and flowering pathways.
Core circadian clock genes implicated as mediators of twilight sensing and downstream regulation of growth and flowering responses in Arabidopsis.
A metabolic process involving reactive oxygen species homeostasis and turnover, identified by transcriptome and proteome analyses as being influenced by twilight length.
The light-driven energy-conversion process in plants that was found to be affected by twilight length at the transcriptomic and proteomic levels.
Plant metabolic processing of carbon compounds, reported as one of the biological processes altered by twilight length.
A phytochrome photoreceptor implicated in the twilight sensing pathway upstream of LHY/CCA1 and flowering modulation.
A phytochrome photoreceptor identified as part of the twilight sensing pathway that transmits light information to circadian and flowering regulators.
A phytochrome photoreceptor involved in the proposed twilight sensing pathway affecting downstream developmental regulation.
A cryptochrome photoreceptor participating in the twilight sensing pathway and contributing to light perception upstream of LHY/CCA1.
A flowering-regulatory signaling pathway downstream of LHY/CCA1 that mediates modulation of flowering time in response to twilight length.

The endogenous timekeeping system in Arabidopsis that coordinates rhythmic gene expression and oscillator function. It is the broader biological process within which TOC1, LHY, and CCA1 interact to maintain clock regulation.
Genes involved in circadian timing regulation. In this text, they include LHY, CCA1, and TOC1, which interact to control oscillator function and feedback regulation.

A MYB transcription factor and Arabidopsis clock gene that participates in circadian regulation. It negatively regulates TOC1 expression and is itself positively regulated by TOC1 in the described feedback loop.

A MYB transcription factor and Arabidopsis clock gene involved in circadian feedback regulation. It negatively regulates TOC1 expression and is positively regulated by TOC1, contributing to clock function.

An Arabidopsis clock gene that functions in reciprocal regulation with LHY and CCA1. It is negatively regulated by LHY and CCA1 and appears to positively regulate their expression, supporting circadian oscillator function.
A transcription factor family to which LHY and CCA1 belong. These proteins bind promoter regions and regulate gene expression in the circadian clock network.
The promoter region of the TOC1 gene that contains a regulatory region critical for clock regulation. It is bound by LHY and CCA1 to mediate negative regulation of TOC1 expression.
The functional operation of the circadian oscillator. The reciprocal interactions among LHY, CCA1, and TOC1 are described as central and critical for this process.
The overall functional output of the Arabidopsis circadian clock. The feedback loop formed by LHY, CCA1, and TOC1 is stated to be critical for this function.
The plant model organism studied in this paper; it serves as the biological subject in which circadian rhythm regulation by LHY and CCA1 is investigated.
A related MYB-like transcription factor in Arabidopsis that functions as a negative regulatory element in the circadian clock and is required for maintenance of circadian rhythms.
A related MYB-like transcription factor in Arabidopsis that acts with LHY as a partially redundant negative regulator of the central circadian oscillator.
The transcription factor family to which LHY and CCA1 belong; these factors are implicated in circadian regulation and oscillator function.
The endogenous rhythmic biological process being regulated in Arabidopsis; the paper focuses on its maintenance, period, and phase under different light conditions.
The core circadian clock mechanism whose function depends on LHY and CCA1 and which generates circadian rhythmicity in gene expression and leaf movement.
A circadian output and regulatory process measured in the study; changes in its timing reflect altered clock function in lhy and cca1 mutants.
A circadian behavioral/physiological output in Arabidopsis used as evidence of altered rhythm period after LHY inactivation.
Genetically engineered Arabidopsis plants lacking both LHY and CCA1 function; used to test redundancy and essentiality for circadian rhythm maintenance.
An environmental light condition under which circadian rhythm maintenance was assessed; it reveals the requirement for LHY and CCA1 in sustaining rhythms.
An environmental photoperiod setting used to examine phase changes in circadian gene expression in mutant plants.
A circadian-associated gene whose expression phase becomes dramatically earlier in lhy cca1-1 plants under light/dark cycles.
A circadian-associated gene whose expression phase becomes dramatically earlier in lhy cca1-1 plants under light/dark cycles.

CIRCADIAN CLOCK-ASSOCIATED 1, a core clock protein that associates with the EE of the VREVIN3 cis-element and participates in activating VIN3 transcription during vernalization. Its abundance and transcript oscillation are altered during prolonged cold, linking circadian regulation to cold-responsive flowering competence.

LATE-ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL, a core clock protein that binds the EE of the VREVIN3 cis-element and contributes to VIN3 transcriptional activation during vernalization. It functions with CCA1 in long-term cold sensing and vernalization response regulation.

VERNALIZATION INSENSITIVE 3, a vernalization-induced gene whose transcription is upregulated by long-term cold in Arabidopsis. It is central to the vernalization response and flowering competence, and its expression depends on the VREVIN3 promoter element and clock proteins CCA1/LHY.

A vernalization-responsive cis-element in the VIN3 promoter composed of a G-box and an evening element (EE). It mediates cold-induced VIN3 transcription and serves as the binding region for CCA1 and LHY at the EE.

A promoter cis-regulatory motif within VREVIN3 that contributes to full induction of VIN3 expression during vernalization. Mutation of the G-box impairs vernalization-responsive transcriptional activation.

A promoter cis-regulatory motif within VREVIN3 that is associated with binding of CCA1 and LHY. It is required for full VIN3 induction during vernalization and links circadian clock regulation to cold-responsive transcription.

A long-term cold-mediated process that confers flowering competence in plants. In this study it regulates VIN3 induction, depends on promoter cis-elements and clock proteins, and is impaired when VIN3 activation is disrupted.

A prolonged cold exposure scenario that triggers vernalization-associated transcriptional changes, including VIN3 induction and altered CCA1/LHY oscillations. It is the environmental stimulus underlying the study's regulatory mechanism.

Extended cold exposure during which CCA1/LHY transcript oscillations are altered and CCA1 abundance increases at dusk. It provides the temporal context for cold-mediated VIN3 activation and flowering acceleration.

entity_name: MILD COLD CONDITIONS SUCH AS AT 12°C
description: A milder long-term cold exposure condition highlighted as especially revealing the impaired VIN3 induction and flowering acceleration in the cca1 lhy double mutant background. It represents a specific temperature context for vernalization sensitivity.

The developmental outcome acquired through vernalization, enabling plants to flower after prolonged cold exposure. It is regulated by VIN3 induction and affected by disruptions in CCA1/LHY-mediated control.
The transcriptional output of the VIN3 gene, measured as induction under vernalization. It is the key molecular endpoint controlled by VREVIN3, CCA1, and LHY.
The physiological response to prolonged cold that includes proper VIN3 induction and flowering competence. Mutations in VREVIN3 motifs and loss of CCA1/LHY function lead to defects in this endpoint.
A developmental outcome promoted by long-term cold-mediated VIN3 induction. It is impaired in the cca1 lhy double mutant background, especially under mild cold conditions.
The transcript oscillation profile of the core clock genes CCA1 and LHY during prolonged cold exposure. Their altered rhythmicity indicates cold-induced modulation of circadian regulation.

The protein level of CCA1, which increases at dusk during prolonged cold exposure and coincides with the diurnal peak of VIN3 transcripts. This abundance change supports a mechanistic link to VIN3 activation.

A functional allele mentioned as part of the genetic background used to assess cold-mediated VIN3 induction and flowering acceleration. It provides a permissive context for vernalization-related regulation.

A plant genetic background lacking both CCA1 and LHY function, used to test the role of these clock proteins in vernalization. It shows impaired VIN3 induction and reduced flowering acceleration under long-term cold, especially mild cold.
The plant species in which VIN3-mediated vernalization regulation is studied. It serves as the biological model for examining cold-responsive flowering competence and clock-gene control.
The plant model organism studied in this paper; it serves as the biological subject in which circadian-clock genes and flowering-time regulation are analyzed.

An extremely early flowering mutant genotype of Arabidopsis thaliana used as an experimental subject to probe genetic interactions among clock-associated genes and their effects on photoperiodic flowering.
The endogenous timekeeping process that measures day length and regulates downstream photoperiodic responses, including flowering-time control and output pathways.
The day-length-dependent biological pathway controlling flowering time; it is modulated by circadian-clock components and linked to CO-FT signaling.
A canonical flowering-time output pathway involving CO and FT expression, used here as the downstream pathway linked to circadian-clock regulation.

A conceptual model explaining photoperiodic control by requiring coincidence between internal circadian phase and external day length; used as the interpretive framework for flowering-time regulation.
A major circadian clock-associated gene/protein acting as an upstream activator in the genetic circuitry controlling photoperiodic flowering.
A circadian clock-associated gene/protein that functions redundantly with LHY as a negative regulator of the photoperiodic flowering pathway.
A circadian clock-associated gene/protein that functions redundantly with CCA1 as a negative regulator of the photoperiodic flowering pathway.
A flowering-associated gene whose expression profile was examined in mutants to assess linkage between the circadian clock and the CO-FT output pathway.
A flowering-associated gene whose expression profile was examined in mutants to assess circadian-clock control of the CO-FT output pathway.
A flowering-associated gene whose phase control is described as crucial for linking the circadian clock to the photoperiodic output pathway.
A flowering-associated gene implicated in phase control that is considered crucial for the linkage between the circadian clock and photoperiodic flowering output.
A flowering-associated gene implicated in phase control that is considered crucial for the linkage between the circadian clock and photoperiodic flowering output.
A core circadian-clock regulatory mechanism involving reciprocal inhibition/feedback among clock components, discussed as compatible with the TOC1-CCA1/LHY genetic linkage.
A regulatory feedback mechanism mentioned as part of the core circadian-clock architecture and linked conceptually to the TOC1-CCA1/LHY circuitry.
An early photomorphogenic downstream pathway referenced as another output pathway that the circadian clock may open during the night-time.
The plant model organism studied in this paper, serving as the biological system in which circadian clock gene regulation and histone modification mechanisms are investigated.
A core gene regulatory system that generates and maintains circadian rhythms; it is the central biological process under study and is regulated by transcriptional and chromatin-based mechanisms.
The endogenous rhythmic biological output maintained by the circadian clock; it represents the functional endpoint of the oscillator gene network.
CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1, a morning-expressed circadian clock regulator that negatively regulates TOC1 and participates in feedback control of clock gene expression.
LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL, a morning-expressed circadian clock regulator that functions with CCA1 to repress TOC1 and shape circadian transcriptional feedback.
TIMING OF CAB EXPRESSION 1, an evening-expressed circadian clock gene that is repressed by CCA1/LHY and also represses CCA1 and LHY expression through promoter binding.
Chromatin-level regulatory changes that influence circadian clock gene expression; the paper focuses on histone demethylation and deacetylation as mechanisms controlling oscillator genes.
A class of histone demethylating enzymes related to LSD1, represented here by LDL1 and LDL2, that interact with circadian regulators to repress TOC1 expression.
An LSD1-like histone demethylase in Arabidopsis that interacts with CCA1/LHY and HDA6 to repress TOC1 and regulate circadian clock genes.
An LSD1-like histone demethylase in Arabidopsis that interacts with CCA1/LHY and HDA6 and contributes to TOC1 repression through chromatin modification.
A histone deacetylase that interacts with LDL1 and LDL2 to co-regulate TOC1 expression via histone deacetylation, contributing to circadian gene control.
A genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing method used to identify LDL1 target genes and infer its role in circadian rhythm regulation.

entity_name: SUBSET OF GENES INVOLVED IN THE CIRCADIAN RHYTHM
description: A group of circadian rhythm-related genes identified as LDL1 targets, indicating broader transcriptional regulation beyond TOC1.
The plant organism used as the biological subject in this study. It provides the cellular and developmental context for examining circadian clock transcriptional repression and DET1 function.

An evolutionarily conserved protein complex implicated in transcriptional repression and photomorphogenesis control. In this text it serves as the molecular complex containing DET1 and is linked to repression functions in the plant circadian clock.

A component of the CDD complex that possesses transcriptional repression activity. It physically interacts with CCA1 and LHY, associates with target gene promoters, and is required for repression in the circadian clock context.
A closely related MYB transcription factor and core component of the plant circadian clock. It interacts with DET1 and helps recruit repression machinery to target promoters such as TOC1.
A closely related MYB transcription factor and core component of the plant circadian clock. It physically interacts with DET1 and participates in CCA1/LHY-dependent repression of target genes.
A transcription factor family to which CCA1 and LHY belong. In this study they are the interacting partners of DET1 and function as central circadian clock regulators.
The endogenous timekeeping process in plants that coordinates rhythmic gene expression. The study focuses on how DET1 and the CDD complex mediate transcriptional repression within this process.
A light-dependent developmental process in plants that is repressed by the CDD complex. It is mentioned as a known functional context for COP10-DET1-DDB1 activity.
The regulatory process of suppressing gene transcription. DET1 is shown to have this activity and to be required for repression of target genes in the circadian clock.
A target gene associated with CCA1/LHY-dependent regulation. DET1 associates with its promoter and contributes to its repression in the circadian clock network.
A functional grouping referring to core circadian clock regulators such as CCA1 and LHY. These components recruit DET1 to regulate clock gene expression.
A functional role describing a factor that represses transcription by cooperating with transcription factors. The CDD complex is proposed to function in this capacity across diverse processes.
The advancement and maintenance of circadian timing. DET1 is described as a core transcriptional repression factor important for this process.

The plant species used as the biological subject in this genetics study of circadian clock regulation. It provides the organismal context in which TOC1, CCA1, and LHY function and where rhythmic outputs such as flowering and photomorphogenesis are assessed.

A core circadian clock gene/protein in Arabidopsis thaliana implicated in the central oscillator. It is studied for its genetic interaction with TOC1 and LHY and for its role in regulating floral induction, photomorphogenesis, and rhythmic output.

A core circadian clock gene/protein in Arabidopsis thaliana that functions with CCA1 in the central oscillator. It is part of the genetic network controlling rhythmic activity, floral transition, and photomorphogenic processes.

A central circadian clock gene/protein in Arabidopsis thaliana that interacts genetically with CCA1 and LHY. It contributes to circadian oscillator function and regulates floral transition and output processes.
The core circadian clock mechanism proposed to be formed by CCA1, LHY, and TOC1. It drives rhythmic outputs and is essential for correct circadian output regulation.

The endogenous timing system in Arabidopsis thaliana that governs rhythmic activity and downstream outputs. In this study, it is the broader biological process whose core oscillator is genetically dissected.
Circadian-regulated downstream biological outputs driven by the clock genes. The text specifically includes seasonal control of flowering and photomorphogenesis as examples.
A circadian output process regulating flowering timing in response to seasonal cues. It is described as one of the rhythmic outputs driven by CCA1, LHY, and TOC1.
A light-regulated developmental process in Arabidopsis thaliana that is controlled by the circadian clock network. The study indicates that CCA1/LHY act upstream of TOC1 in regulating this process.
The biological transition toward flowering, examined here as a clock-regulated process. The study tests the genetic relationship between TOC1 and CCA1/LHY in this process.
The developmental switch to flowering, described as being regulated by TOC1 in a CCA1/LHY-dependent manner. It is a key circadian output process in the paper.
The observable circadian rhythmic behavior measured in mutant combinations. It was dramatically attenuated in the cca1 lhy toc1 triple mutant, indicating strong dependence on the clock genes.
The regulation of downstream outputs by the circadian clock. The study uses genetic mutants to test how CCA1/LHY and TOC1 contribute to this regulatory function.

A genetically engineered Arabidopsis mutant lacking CCA1, LHY, and TOC1 function. It serves as an experimental subject used to assess the combined effect of these genes on rhythmic activity and clock output.
A genetically engineered Arabidopsis mutant combination lacking CCA1 and TOC1 function. It is used to probe pairwise genetic interactions in circadian and output regulation.
A genetically engineered Arabidopsis mutant combination lacking LHY and TOC1 function. It is used to test genetic relationships in circadian output and photomorphogenic regulation.
The experimental approach used to construct mutants and infer gene relationships in the circadian network. It provides the basis for the direct experimental support described in the abstract.
Conceptual models of circadian clock organization that were tested against mutant data. They are used to interpret the genetic interactions among CCA1, LHY, and TOC1.

Model plant organism used as the experimental subject in this study of circadian rhythmicity. It provides the biological context in which CCA1 and LHY function, mutant phenotypes are assessed, and sustained oscillations are measured under different light conditions.
Arabidopsis mutant plants lacking CCA1 protein. This subject group is used to evaluate the effect of CCA1 loss on circadian period and gene expression, especially under constant light conditions.

Double mutant Arabidopsis plants lacking CCA1 and with LHY function strongly reduced. This experimental population is used to test whether circadian oscillations can be maintained when both major clock components are compromised.
An experimental environmental setting in which plants are assayed without dark transitions. It is used to reveal short-period phenotypes and loss of sustained oscillations in circadian clock mutants.
An experimental environmental setting with continuous darkness. It is used to assess whether circadian oscillations can be maintained independently of external light cues.

A cyclic environmental setting with alternating light and dark periods. It provides entraining conditions under which Arabidopsis circadian function persists even when CCA1 and LHY activities are reduced.

Endogenous autoregulatory timing mechanisms that coordinate biological activities with 24-hour environmental cycles. In this paper, they are the central process whose rhythmicity depends on CCA1 and LHY.
The sustained rhythmic behavior of the circadian clock. The title and abstract indicate that maintaining this rhythmicity is the key biological outcome influenced by CCA1 and LHY.

Rhythmic clock-related oscillatory behavior observed in mutant and wild-type plants. The study specifically evaluates whether sustained oscillations can be maintained under constant light and constant darkness.
Gene expression phenotype used as a readout of circadian clock function. In cca1-1 plants, several genes show a short-period expression pattern under constant light.
Altered circadian timing phenotype characterized by a faster clock pace and shortened period. It is observed in cca1-1 plants when gene expression is assayed under constant light conditions.
CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1, a transcription factor and core circadian clock component in Arabidopsis. It is implicated in maintaining rhythmicity and overlaps functionally with LHY.
LATE ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL, a transcription factor and core circadian clock component in Arabidopsis. It partially compensates for loss of CCA1 and contributes to sustaining circadian oscillations.
The protein product of CCA1, absent in cca1-1 plants. Its loss is associated with altered circadian period and reduced clock robustness.
The functional activity of LHY in the circadian clock. The abstract indicates that this activity can partially compensate for CCA1 loss but is insufficient when strongly reduced in the double mutant.
Regulatory proteins represented here by CCA1 and LHY. They are described as overlapping components of the Arabidopsis circadian clock and are functionally important for clock maintenance.

A WRKY transcription factor protein that participates in circadian regulation of PIF4 expression. It forms heterodimers with WRKY10, interacts with CCA1/LHY and phyB, and contributes to targeting of the PIF4 promoter and maintenance of PIF4 expression timing.

A WRKY transcription factor protein involved in photomorphogenesis and circadian control of PIF4. It heterodimerizes with WRKY2, interacts with CCA1/LHY and phyB, and helps sustain proper PIF4 promoter targeting and expression peaks.

A critical signaling hub whose expression and accumulation show circadian peaks in the morning and afternoon. It is regulated by WRKY2/WRKY10, CCA1/LHY, SHB1, and phyB, and its promoter is a key target of these interactions.

A circadian transcriptional regulator complex referenced as binding the MYB element near the PIF4 promoter under red and blue light. It directly interacts with WRKY2 and WRKY10 and is targeted to the PIF4 promoter to regulate circadian expression.

A phytochrome photoreceptor that interacts with WRKY2 and WRKY10. Its interaction enhances targeting of CCA1 and LHY to the PIF4 promoter, linking light perception to circadian transcriptional regulation.

A regulatory factor that associates with the WRKY2 and WRKY10 loci and enhances their expression. It participates in a forward regulatory loop that sustains WRKY protein accumulation and supports PIF4 expression peaks.
The promoter region of the PIF4 gene that contains a target site near a MYB element. It is bound or targeted by WRKY2/WRKY10 and CCA1/LHY, making it central to circadian transcriptional control.
A promoter element near the PIF4 promoter target site that is bound by CCA1 and LHY under red and blue light. It serves as a cis-regulatory feature involved in transcriptional regulation of PIF4.
A light-dependent developmental process in which WRKY2 and WRKY10 are reported to have regulatory functions. It provides the broader biological context for their control of PIF4 expression.

The time-of-day-dependent transcriptional pattern of PIF4, characterized by morning and afternoon peaks and maintenance toward noon and afternoon. It is regulated by WRKY2, WRKY10, CCA1/LHY, phyB, and SHB1.
The transcriptional output of the PIF4 gene, described as peaking in the morning and afternoon and being sustained by a forward regulatory loop. It is the main regulated process in the study.
The abundance of PIF4 protein, which also peaks in the morning and afternoon. It reflects downstream regulation of PIF4 beyond transcription and contributes to circadian signaling output.

entity_name: TARGETING OF CCA1 AND LHY TO THE PIF4 PROMOTER
description: A regulatory process in which CCA1 and LHY are recruited to the PIF4 promoter, enhanced by WRKY2/WRKY10 and phyB interactions. This targeting is essential for maintaining optimal PIF4 expression timing.

A self-reinforcing regulatory circuit in which SHB1 enhances WRKY2/WRKY10 expression, sustaining WRKY accumulation and continued targeting of CCA1/LHY to the PIF4 locus. It stabilizes circadian PIF4 regulation.

Light conditions under which CCA1 and LHY bind the MYB element near the PIF4 promoter. In this plant biology context, it functions as the environmental light exposure scenario shaping transcriptional regulation.

The observed temporal expression pattern of PIF4 across the day, which is maintained by WRKY2/WRKY10, CCA1/LHY, phyB, and SHB1. It represents the functional endpoint of the regulatory network described.
The plant model organism studied in this paper, serving as the biological system in which circadian clock regulation and kinase-dependent posttranslational modification were examined.

A family of Arabidopsis kinases implicated in posttranslational regulation of the plant circadian clock; multiple CKL proteins are inhibited by PHA767491 and are functionally linked to period length control.
A chemical inhibitor originally described as an animal CDC7/CDK9 inhibitor, used here as a probe to perturb Arabidopsis CKL activity and alter circadian period length.
The originally proposed kinase targets of PHA767491 in animals; in this study, they are contrasted with CKL proteins as the actual binding/inhibition targets in Arabidopsis.
An experimental approach combining chemical screening and chemical probe-based affinity proteomics to identify kinase targets and infer functional effects on the circadian clock.
A screening method used to identify compounds that alter the Arabidopsis circadian period, including the period-lengthening effect of PHA767491.
A proteomic assay using a chemical probe to identify protein binding partners of PHA767491 and establish CKL proteins as the relevant targets.
A probe used in affinity proteomics to capture and identify proteins bound by PHA767491, enabling target deconvolution.
The endogenous timekeeping process regulating daily and seasonal adaptation; in this study it is modulated by CKL family activity and PHA767491 treatment.
A regulatory mechanism affecting clock function in plants; CKL family proteins participate in this process by phosphorylating clock repressors.
Core circadian regulatory loops in eukaryotes and the plant clock, where transcriptional repressors and their phosphorylation state influence clock timing.
The kinase-mediated posttranslational modification performed by CKL4 on PRR5 and TOC1, central to regulation of circadian clock components.
A member of the Arabidopsis CKL family that phosphorylates the transcriptional repressors PRR5 and TOC1 in the circadian TTFL.
A transcriptional repressor in the Arabidopsis circadian TTFL that is phosphorylated by CKL4 and accumulates after PHA767491 treatment.
A transcriptional repressor in the Arabidopsis circadian TTFL that is phosphorylated by CKL4 and accumulates after PHA767491 treatment.
Downstream genes regulated by PRR5 and TOC1 whose expression decreases following PHA767491 treatment, reflecting altered circadian transcriptional repression.
The measurable timing phenotype of the Arabidopsis clock that is lengthened by PHA767491 and by CKL knockdown.
A treatment-associated increase in PRR5 and TOC1 abundance observed after PHA767491 exposure, indicating altered protein turnover or stabilization.

entity_name: DECREASING EXPRESSION OF PRR5- AND TOC1-TARGET GENES
description: A downstream transcriptional outcome observed after PHA767491 treatment, consistent with enhanced repression by accumulated PRR5 and TOC1.

entity_name: SIMULTANEOUS KNOCKDOWN OF ARABIDOPSIS CKL-ENCODING GENES
description: A genetic perturbation used to reduce CKL family function, producing circadian period lengthening and supporting the role of CKLs in clock regulation.
A mutant Arabidopsis genotype lacking both PRR5 and TOC1, used to test genetic sensitivity to PHA767491-induced period lengthening.
A reduced response phenotype observed in the prr5 toc1 double mutant, indicating that PRR5 and TOC1 contribute to the compound's period-lengthening effect.
